title: Why Gaelic pronunciation deserves extra attention
body: Gaelic spelling is actually very regular once you know the rules, but the rules are different enough from English that guessing from the letters alone will mislead you. A handful of core patterns (broad/slender consonants, vowel length, lenition, pre-aspiration) explain almost everything — learn those patterns rather than trying to memorise each word's sound individually.

title: Broad vs slender consonants (caol ri caol, leathann ri leathann)
body: Every consonant in Gaelic comes in two versions: 'broad' (pronounced further back in the mouth, roughly like English but deeper/rounder) and 'slender' (pronounced further forward, with a slight 'y'-like quality). You can tell which version a consonant is just by looking at the vowel letters next to it: a, o, u make a consonant broad; e, i make it slender. This is why Gaelic spelling always keeps a broad vowel next to a broad vowel and a slender vowel next to a slender vowel around the same consonant — the vowel letters are there partly to mark the consonant's quality, not just their own sound.
tips: Broad c (next to a/o/u, as in 'cas') sounds closer to English 'k' in 'call'.
Slender c (next to e/i, as in 'cir') sounds noticeably fronted, almost like 'k' + a quick 'y'.
When in doubt reading a new word, check the vowel immediately before/after the consonant to guess broad vs slender.

title: Vowel length changes meaning, not just emphasis
body: Gaelic distinguishes short and long vowels the way English distinguishes 'ship' and 'sheep' — it's not a stylistic choice, it can be the only difference between two different words. The grave accent (à, ò, ù, etc.) marks a long vowel. Skipping vowel length is one of the most common beginner mistakes and the single easiest thing to fix once you're aware of it.
tips: cas (short a) = foot/leg, càs (long à) = predicament/crisis — different words.
When you see a grave accent, hold the vowel noticeably longer than an unaccented one.

title: Lenition softens the sound, not just the spelling
body: Lenition (adding 'h' after the first consonant — mo mhàthair, a bhean) is a real change in how the sound is made, usually making it softer/more open, not a silent spelling quirk. 'Bh' and 'mh' are both pronounced like an English 'v' (or a soft 'w' in some dialects/positions), 'dh' and 'gh' become a soft, almost swallowed glide, and 'fh' usually disappears entirely (becomes silent). Recognising lenited consonants as different sounds — not the base letter plus a silent h — is key to sounding natural.
tips: mo fhacal (my word) — the 'fh' is silent, so it sounds like 'mo acal'.
a dhuine (o man, vocative) — 'dh' is a soft glide, not a hard 'd' or 'g'.

title: Pre-aspiration: the 'puff' comes before c, p, t — not after
body: In English, the little puff of air after c/p/t (aspiration) comes after the consonant ('pin' has a puff right after the p). In Gaelic, when c, p or t appears in the middle or end of a word, that puff of air shifts to come *before* the consonant instead — this is called pre-aspiration, and it's one of the most distinctive, recognisable features of a Gaelic accent. It's strongest before 'c' (sounds like a light 'ch'/'kh' sound right before the k), and lighter (closer to a simple 'h') before 't' and 'p'.
tips: mac is pronounced closer to 'machk' than a flat 'mak'.

This feature is shared with only a handful of world languages (Icelandic, Sámi, some Inuit languages) — it's genuinely unusual and worth practising deliberately rather than assuming English habits will transfer.

title: Common silent/surprising letter combinations
body: A short list of spelling patterns that look confusing from an English-reading habit but are completely regular in Gaelic once learned: 'fh' is silent almost everywhere; 'bh'/'mh' = a 'v' sound; 'dh'/'gh' = a soft glide (or silent at the end of a word); 'sh'/'th' = an English 'h' sound; double vowels with a hyphen-like 'a-i', 'e-a' etc. often signal a glide between two vowel qualities rather than two separate vowel sounds.
tips: a Sheumais (vocative of Seumas/James) — 'Sh' sounds like English 'h'.
laogh (calf) ends in a silent/near-silent 'gh' — closer to 'lœ:' than 'laog'.
